# projective_grid - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/projective-grid/0.10.0/projective_grid/

## Expand description

Target-agnostic projective grid recovery primitives.

This crate is intentionally small at the public boundary. It models two lattice families, two tasks, and explicit evidence shapes. Target-specific identifiers and detector classes belong in caller crates and should be converted into generic point features or coordinate hypotheses before entering this crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#design-references)Design references

The crate is organised around three orthogonal axes — lattice family,
recovery strategy, and input-feature kind. The architecture and the
orientation-as-an-optional-cue model are documented under `docs/` in the
crate source tree:

- `docs/DESIGN.md`— the three design axes, the shared pipeline back-half, and how the lattice family extends to hex.
- `docs/ORIENTATION.md`— where each strategy consumes per-corner orientation and how each can run orientation-free (the dot-grid path).

The per-strategy stage maps live in `docs/algorithms/topological-grid-detection.md`
(repo root) and `calib-targets-chessboard/docs/PIPELINE.md`.

[§](https://docs.rs#two-public-tiers)Two public tiers

The crate ships an intentional two-tier public API. Both tiers are supported; they differ in audience and in how fast the surface is allowed to move.

[§](https://docs.rs#stable-tier--the-facade-ordinary-users)Stable tier — the facade (ordinary users)

The items re-exported at the crate root are the supported surface for an
ordinary caller who wants to *detect a grid* and read the labels back:

- the entry points `detect_grid``detect_grid_all``check_consistency`
- the request types `Evidence``DetectionParams``DetectionRequest``ConsistencyParams``ConsistencyRequest`
- the result types `GridSolution``LabelledGrid``DetectionReport`
- the lattice model `Lattice``LatticeKind``Coord``PointFeature``OrientedFeature``LocalAxis`
- the orientation-synthesis helpers (`synthesize_oriented2``cluster_axes``AxisClusterCenters``AxisAssignment`

This tier carries normal semver guarantees: breaking changes here go through the usual deprecation cycle.

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-tier--the-composition-api-build-your-own-detector)Advanced tier — the composition API (build your own detector)

[ shared](https://docs.rs/shared/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/topological/index.html)

`topological`[,](https://docs.rs/lattice/index.html)

`lattice`[, and](https://docs.rs/orient/index.html)

`orient`[expose the assembly engine the facade is built from, as a deliberate](https://docs.rs/cluster/index.html)

`cluster`**composition API**. It exists so a consumer with its own per-pattern invariants — the in-workspace chessboard detector is the reference example, but the contract is written for external consumers too — can drive the same grid-growth and recovery machinery under its own policy instead of going through the one-size-fits-all facade. This is intended product, not a private engine that merely happens to be

`pub`.The composition contract — what a consumer supplies and what the engine guarantees in return:

- **You supply a**This is the seam between the geometry-only growth machinery and your pattern’s rules. The policy answers four questions per candidate —- `shared::grow::SquareAttachPolicy`- `is_eligible`,- `required_label_at`,- `accept_candidate`,- `edge_ok`— letting you veto an attachment that is geometrically plausible but illegal for your pattern (e.g. a chessboard’s alternating-colour parity, or a per-corner blacklist). The engine never relabels behind your back: every attachment it proposes has already passed your policy.
- **You drive the growth / recovery engine.**The geometry-only primitives live under- `shared`- `shared::grow`- `shared::fill`- `shared::extension`- `shared::grow_extend`- `shared::recovery_schedule`- `RecoverySchedule`- `RecoveryParams`
- **You compose the shared back-half.**After your front-half has built integer-labelled components, the lattice-parameterised back-half reunites them with local geometry only (- `shared::merge`- `shared::validate`- `Lattice`
- **The guarantees.**Every stage is- *drop-only*with respect to labels: a corner whose geometry does not cohere is removed, never relabelled. The precision contract of the facade —- **zero wrong**, misses acceptable — therefore holds for a consumer that composes the engine under its own policy, because the policy gates and the validate/drop filters run on every attachment exactly as they do on the facade path. Returned components are rebased so the labelled bounding-box minimum is- `(i, j)`labels- `(0, 0)`; quad / homography corner order is TL, TR, BR, BL.

**Stability of the advanced tier.** This surface is *advanced, and may
evolve*: its shape tracks the engine’s internal structure, so an item may
change between minor releases when the engine is refactored. That is a
deliberate product choice — the tier trades a slower-moving contract for
direct access to the engine — not a disclaimer that it is really private.
If you only need to detect a grid, depend on the facade; reach for the
composition tier when you are building a *new kind of detector* on top of
the engine. Engine items with no external consumer stay `pub(crate)`, so
the advanced surface is kept no wider than what a consumer actually
composes.

[§](https://docs.rs#core-vs-extended-surface)Core vs. extended surface

Orthogonal to the stable/advanced split is a second distinction worth making explicit, because the two halves are exercised very differently in practice:

- **Core path (exercised in production).**The square lattice (- `LatticeKind::Square`- `Evidence::Oriented2`
- **Extended path (library-only breadth).**The hexagonal lattice (- `Hex`- `topological`- `D6_TRANSFORMS`- `orient`- `shared::recovery_schedule`- `Evidence::Positions`- `Evidence::Oriented1`- `docs/DESIGN.md`for the full core-vs-extended map.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [check](https://docs.rs/check/index.html)
- Consistency-check task facade.
- [cluster](https://docs.rs/cluster/index.html)
- Global grid-direction recovery from per-feature dual-axis estimates.
- [detect](https://docs.rs/detect/index.html)
- Detection task facade.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error types for grid tasks.
- [feature](https://docs.rs/feature/index.html)
- Generic feature evidence consumed by grid tasks.
- [float](https://docs.rs/float/index.html)
- Sealed `Float`
- [geometry](https://docs.rs/geometry/index.html)
- Geometry helpers shared by grid tasks.
- [lattice](https://docs.rs/lattice/index.html)
- Lattice-family axis: the parameter that the strategies and the shared back-half are written against, rather than a copy per family.
- [orient](https://docs.rs/orient/index.html)
- Local lattice-orientation synthesis from point positions alone.
- [result](https://docs.rs/result/index.html)
- Shared output types for detection and consistency tasks.
- [shared](https://docs.rs/shared/index.html)
- Shared detection back-half plus the geometry-only grid-growth engine.
- [topological](https://docs.rs/topological/index.html)
- Axis-driven topological grid finder (Shu/Brunton/Fiala 2009) for the
`(LatticeKind::Square, Evidence::Oriented2)`slot.

# lash_provider_auth - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lash-provider-auth/0.1.0-alpha.82/lash_provider_auth/

## Expand description

Shared OAuth primitives used by provider crates that implement OAuth-based auth (Codex, Google). API-key backends bypass this module.

Provider-specific endpoints, device-code flows, PKCE helpers, and
refresh logic live in each provider crate under `oauth.rs`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [extract_](https://docs.rs/fn.extract_query_param.html)- query_ - param
- Extract the value of a given query parameter from a URL or raw
query-string. Returns `None`if the key is absent.
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_pkce.html)- pkce
- Generate a PKCE code verifier and challenge pair. PKCE verifier is 32 bytes of OS entropy (via two UUID v4s) base64url-encoded; the challenge is its SHA-256 base64url-encoded.
- [now_](https://docs.rs/fn.now_secs.html)- secs
- [percent_](https://docs.rs/fn.percent_decode.html)- decode
- Percent-decode a query-string value (handles `+`→ space).
- [url_](https://docs.rs/fn.url_form_encode.html)- form_ - encode
- Form-urlencoded body encoder for OAuth token endpoints.
- [urlencoded](https://docs.rs/fn.urlencoded.html)
- Minimal percent-encoding for URL query parameters.

# solana_log_parser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-log-parser/0.1.0/solana_log_parser/

## Expand description

A parser for Solana transaction logs.

Solana runtime logs are a flat, ordered sequence of strings describing
program invocations, their nested inner instructions, and any messages
programs emit along the way (`msg!`, compute unit reports, return data,
etc). This crate turns that flat list into a tree of [ InstructionCall](https://docs.rs/struct.InstructionCall.html)s
that mirrors the actual call structure, so callers can walk invocations
and their children without re-parsing stack height markers themselves.

This crate is `no_std` (with `alloc`) so it can be used in constrained
environments such as on-chain programs or WASM.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let logs: Vec<String> = /* raw transaction logs */;
let instructions = Parser::parse(&logs)?;
for top_level in &instructions {
    for call in top_level.iter() {
        println!("{} at depth {}", call.program_id, call.stack_height);
    }
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Instruction](https://docs.rs/struct.InstructionCall.html)- Call
- A single program invocation, including any nested inner instructions it made and the logs it emitted.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineParser.html)- Parser
- Parses individual log lines that are known to belong to a specific program.
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html)
- Entry point for parsing raw transaction logs into a tree of
`InstructionCall`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorStatus.html)- Status
- Like `Status`
- [Line](https://docs.rs/enum.Line.html)
- The parsed classification of a single raw log line.
- [Log](https://docs.rs/enum.Log.html)
- One entry in an `InstructionCall`
- [LogHint](https://docs.rs/enum.LogHint.html)
- Categorizes what kind of program log a `Log::Program``Program log:`,`Program consumed`).
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)- Error
- Errors that can occur while parsing transaction logs.
- [Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html)
- The outcome of a completed program invocation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)
- Parses a full list of transaction log lines into the top-level instructions (and their nested invocations) they describe.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_line.html)- line
- Classifies a single raw log line into a `Line`

---

# sp_wasm_interface - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sp-wasm-interface/27.0.0/target-redirect/sp_wasm_interface/

## Expand description

Types and traits for interfacing between the host and the wasm runtime.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Extended](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtendedHostFunctions.html)- Host - Functions
- A wrapper which merges two sets of host functions, and allows the second set to override the host functions from the first set.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html)
- Type to represent a pointer in wasm at the host.
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/struct.Signature.html)
- The Signature of a function

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Return](https://docs.rs/enum.ReturnValue.html)- Value
- Typed value that can be returned from a function.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html)
- Values supported by Substrate on the boundary between host/Wasm.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.ValueType.html)- Type
- Value types supported by Substrate on the boundary between host/Wasm.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Function](https://docs.rs/trait.Function.html)
- Something that provides a function implementation on the host for a wasm function.
- [Function](https://docs.rs/trait.FunctionContext.html)- Context
- Context used by `Function`to interact with the allocator and the memory of the wasm instance.
- [Host](https://docs.rs/trait.HostFunctions.html)- Functions
- Something that provides implementations for host functions.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoValue.html)- Value
- Something that can be converted into a wasm compatible `Value`.
- [Maybe](https://docs.rs/trait.MaybeRefUnwindSafe.html)- RefUnwind - Safe
- A trait that requires `RefUnwindSafe`when`feature = std`.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/trait.PointerType.html)- Type
- Something that can be wrapped in a wasm `Pointer`.
- [TryFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.TryFromValue.html)- Value
- Something that can may be created from a wasm `Value`.
- [WasmTy](https://docs.rs/trait.WasmTy.html)
- A trait for types directly usable at the WASM FFI boundary without any conversion at all.

[404](#404)pub struct ExtendedHostFunctions<Base, Overlay> {

[409](#409)
[410](#410)impl<Base, Overlay> HostFunctions for ExtendedHostFunctions<Base, Overlay>
[411](#411)where
[412](#412)	Base: HostFunctions,
[413](#413)	Overlay: HostFunctions,
[414](#414){
[415](#415)	fn host_functions() -> Vec<&'static dyn Function> {
[416](#416)		let mut base = Base::host_functions();
[417](#417)		let overlay = Overlay::host_functions();
[418](#418)		base.retain(|host_fn| {
[419](#419)			!overlay.iter().any(|ext_host_fn| host_fn.name() == ext_host_fn.name())
[420](#420)		});
[421](#421)		base.extend(overlay);
[422](#422)		base
[423](#423)	}
[424](#424)
[425](#425)	if_wasmtime_is_enabled! {
[426](#426)		fn register_static<T>(registry: &mut T) -> core::result::Result<(), T::Error>
[427](#427)		where
[428](#428)			T: HostFunctionRegistry,
[429](#429)		{
[430](#430)			struct Proxy<'a, T> {
[431](#431)				registry: &'a mut T,
[432](#432)				seen_overlay: std::collections::HashSet<String>,
[433](#433)				seen_base: std::collections::HashSet<String>,
[434](#434)				overlay_registered: bool,
[435](#435)			}
[436](#436)
[437](#437)			impl<'a, T> HostFunctionRegistry for Proxy<'a, T>
[438](#438)			where
[439](#439)				T: HostFunctionRegistry,
[440](#440)			{
[441](#441)				type State = T::State;
[442](#442)				type Error = T::Error;
[443](#443)				type FunctionContext = T::FunctionContext;
[444](#444)
[445](#445)				fn with_function_context<R>(
[446](#446)					caller: wasmtime::Caller<Self::State>,
[447](#447)					callback: impl FnOnce(&mut dyn FunctionContext) -> R,
[448](#448)				) -> R {
[449](#449)					T::with_function_context(caller, callback)
[450](#450)				}
[451](#451)
[452](#452)				fn register_static<Params, Results>(
[453](#453)					&mut self,
[454](#454)					fn_name: &str,
[455](#455)					func: impl wasmtime::IntoFunc<Self::State, Params, Results> + 'static,
[456](#456)				) -> core::result::Result<(), Self::Error> {
[457](#457)					if self.overlay_registered {
[458](#458)						if !self.seen_base.insert(fn_name.to_owned()) {
[459](#459)							log::warn!(
[460](#460)								target: "extended_host_functions",
[461](#461)								"Duplicate base host function: '{}'",
[462](#462)								fn_name,
[463](#463)							);
[464](#464)
[465](#465)							return Ok(())
[467](#467)						}
[468](#468)
[469](#469)						if self.seen_overlay.contains(fn_name) {
[470](#470)							log::debug!(
[472](#472)								target: "extended_host_functions",
[473](#473)								"Overriding base host function: '{}'",
[474](#474)								fn_name,
[475](#475)							);
[476](#476)
[477](#477)							return Ok(())
[478](#478)						}
[479](#479)					} else if !self.seen_overlay.insert(fn_name.to_owned()) {
[480](#480)						log::warn!(
[481](#481)							target: "extended_host_functions",
[482](#482)							"Duplicate overlay host function: '{}'",
[483](#483)							fn_name,
[484](#484)						);
[485](#485)
[486](#486)						return Ok(())
[488](#488)					}
[489](#489)
[490](#490)					self.registry.register_static(fn_name, func)
[491](#491)				}
[492](#492)			}
[493](#493)
[494](#494)			let mut proxy = Proxy {
[495](#495)				registry,
[496](#496)				seen_overlay: Default::default(),
[497](#497)				seen_base: Default::default(),
[498](#498)				overlay_registered: false,
[499](#499)			};
[500](#500)
[501](#501)			Overlay::register_static(&mut proxy)?;
[505](#505)			proxy.overlay_registered = true;
[506](#506)			Base::register_static(&mut proxy)?;
[507](#507)
[508](#508)			Ok(())
[509](#509)		}
[510](#510)	}
[511](#511)}
[512](#512)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sp_wasm_interface/lib.rs.html#604)

#### pub const [ENCODED_MAX_SIZE](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.ENCODED_MAX_SIZE): [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html) = 10

Maximum number of bytes `ReturnValue` might occupy when serialized with `SCALE`.

Breakdown: 1 byte for encoding unit/value variant 1 byte for encoding value type 8 bytes for encoding the biggest value types available in wasm: f64, i64.

# Value in sp_wasm_interface - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sp-wasm-interface/27.0.0/sp_wasm_interface/enum.Value.html

## Expand description

Values supported by Substrate on the boundary between host/Wasm.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.I32)

### I32([i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html))

A 32-bit integer.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.I64)

### I64([i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html))

A 64-bit integer.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.F32)

### F32([u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html))

A 32-bit floating-point number stored as raw bit pattern.

You can materialize this value using `f32::from_bits`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.F64)

### F64([u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html))

A 64-bit floating-point number stored as raw bit pattern.

You can materialize this value using `f64::from_bits`.

# ValueType in sp_wasm_interface - Rust

# Enum ValueType

[Source](../src/sp_wasm_interface/lib.rs.html#54-63) ```
pub enum ValueType {
    I32,
    I64,
    F32,
    F64,
}
```

## Expand description

Value types supported by Substrate on the boundary between host/Wasm.

Performs copy-assignment from

`source`.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html#method.clone_from)

Formats the value using the given formatter.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html#tymethod.fmt)

Converts to this type from the input type.

Tests for `self` and `other` values to be equal, and is used by `==`.

Tests for `!=`. The default implementation is almost always sufficient,
and should not be overridden without very good reason.

The type returned in the event of a conversion error.

Performs the conversion.

Immutably borrows from an owned value.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html#tymethod.borrow)

Mutably borrows from an owned value.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.BorrowMut.html#tymethod.borrow_mut)

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`clone_to_uninit`)

Performs copy-assignment from

`self` to

`dest`.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.CloneToUninit.html#tymethod.clone_to_uninit)

Returns the argument unchanged.

Calls `U::from(self)`.

That is, this conversion is whatever the implementation of
[From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)<T> for U

The resulting type after obtaining ownership.

Creates owned data from borrowed data, usually by cloning.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/borrow/trait.ToOwned.html#tymethod.to_owned)

Uses borrowed data to replace owned data, usually by cloning.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/borrow/trait.ToOwned.html#method.clone_into)

The type returned in the event of a conversion error.

Performs the conversion.

The type returned in the event of a conversion error.

Performs the conversion.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Read memory into the given `dest` buffer from `address`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sp_wasm_interface/lib.rs.html#334)#### fn [register_panic_error_message](https://docs.rs#tymethod.register_panic_error_message)(&mut self, message: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sp_wasm_interface/lib.rs.html#334)

#### fn [register_panic_error_message](https://docs.rs#tymethod.register_panic_error_message)(&mut self, message: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html))

Registers a panic error message within the executor.

This is meant to be used in situations where the runtime encounters an unrecoverable error and intends to panic.

Panicking in WASM is done through the [ unreachable](https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/syntax/instructions.html#syntax-instr-control)
instruction which causes an unconditional trap and immediately aborts
the execution. It does not however allow for any diagnostics to be
passed through to the host, so while we do know that

*something*went wrong we don’t have any direct indication of what

*exactly*went wrong.

As a workaround we use this method right before the execution is actually aborted to pass an error message to the host so that it can associate it with the next trap, and return that to the caller.

A WASM trap should be triggered immediately after calling this method; otherwise the error message might be associated with a completely unrelated trap.

It should only be called once, however calling it more than once is harmless and will overwrite the previously set error message.

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# sp_wasm_interface - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sp-wasm-interface/latest/sp_wasm_interface/

## Expand description

Types and traits for interfacing between the host and the wasm runtime.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Extended](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtendedHostFunctions.html)- Host - Functions
- A wrapper which merges two sets of host functions, and allows the second set to override the host functions from the first set.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/struct.Pointer.html)
- Type to represent a pointer in wasm at the host.
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/struct.Signature.html)
- The Signature of a function

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Return](https://docs.rs/enum.ReturnValue.html)- Value
- Typed value that can be returned from a function.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html)
- Values supported by Substrate on the boundary between host/Wasm.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.ValueType.html)- Type
- Value types supported by Substrate on the boundary between host/Wasm.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Function](https://docs.rs/trait.Function.html)
- Something that provides a function implementation on the host for a wasm function.
- [Function](https://docs.rs/trait.FunctionContext.html)- Context
- Context used by `Function`to interact with the allocator and the memory of the wasm instance.
- [Host](https://docs.rs/trait.HostFunctions.html)- Functions
- Something that provides implementations for host functions.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoValue.html)- Value
- Something that can be converted into a wasm compatible `Value`.
- [Maybe](https://docs.rs/trait.MaybeRefUnwindSafe.html)- RefUnwind - Safe
- A trait that requires `RefUnwindSafe`when`feature = std`.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/trait.PointerType.html)- Type
- Something that can be wrapped in a wasm `Pointer`.
- [TryFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.TryFromValue.html)- Value
- Something that can may be created from a wasm `Value`.
- [WasmTy](https://docs.rs/trait.WasmTy.html)
- A trait for types directly usable at the WASM FFI boundary without any conversion at all.

---

# anyhow 1.0.103 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/anyhow/^1.0.81

# Anyhow ¯\_(°ペ)_/¯

This library provides [ anyhow::Error](https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0/anyhow/struct.Error.html), a trait object based error type
for easy idiomatic error handling in Rust applications.

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Details

-
Use `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`, or equivalently`anyhow::Result<T>`, as the return type of any fallible function.Within the function, use `?`to easily propagate any error that implements the`std::error::Error``use Result;`
-
Attach context to help the person troubleshooting the error understand where things went wrong. A low-level error like "No such file or directory" can be annoying to debug without more context about what higher level step the application was in the middle of. `use ;``Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
-
Downcasting is supported and can be by value, by shared reference, or by mutable reference as needed. `// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a // tombstone instead of the content. match root_cause.`
-
If using Rust ≥ 1.65, a backtrace is captured and printed with the error if the underlying error type does not already provide its own. In order to see backtraces, they must be enabled through the environment variables described in `std::backtrace`- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only errors to have backtraces, set `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only panics to have backtraces, set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`and`RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`.

- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
-
Anyhow works with any error type that has an impl of `std::error::Error`, including ones defined in your crate. We do not bundle a`derive(Error)`macro but you can write the impls yourself or use a standalone macro like[thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror).`use Error;`
-
One-off error messages can be constructed using the `anyhow!`macro, which supports string interpolation and produces an`anyhow::Error`.`return Err;`A `bail!`macro is provided as a shorthand for the same early return.`bail!;`

## No-std support

In no_std mode, almost all of the same API is available and works the same way. To depend on Anyhow in no_std mode, disable our default enabled "std" feature in Cargo.toml. A global allocator is required.

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0",  = false }
```
With versions of Rust older than 1.81, no_std mode may require an additional
`.map_err(Error::msg)` when working with a non-Anyhow error type inside a
function that returns Anyhow's error type, as the trait that `?`-based error
conversions are defined by is only available in std in those old versions.

## Comparison to failure

The `anyhow::Error` type works something like `failure::Error`, but unlike
failure ours is built around the standard library's `std::error::Error` trait
rather than a separate trait `failure::Fail`. The standard library has adopted
the necessary improvements for this to be possible as part of [RFC 2504](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/2504-fix-error.md).

## Comparison to thiserror

Use Anyhow if you don't care what error type your functions return, you just
want it to be easy. This is common in application code. Use [thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror) if you
are a library that wants to design your own dedicated error type(s) so that on
failures the caller gets exactly the information that you choose.

# parity-scale-codec 3.7.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/parity-scale-codec/^3.7.5

# Parity SCALE Codec

Rust implementation of the SCALE (Simple Concatenated Aggregate Little-Endian) data format for types used in the Parity Substrate framework.

SCALE is a light-weight format which allows encoding (and decoding) which makes it highly suitable for resource-constrained execution environments like blockchain runtimes and low-power, low-memory devices.

It is important to note that the encoding context (knowledge of how the types and data structures look) needs to be known separately at both encoding and decoding ends. The encoded data does not include this contextual information.

To get a better understanding of how the encoding is done for different types,
take a look at the ["Type encoding (SCALE)" page in Substrate docs](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/scale-codec/).

## Implementation

The codec is implemented using the following traits:

### Encode

The `Encode` trait is used for encoding of data into the SCALE format. The `Encode` trait
contains the following functions:

- `size_hint(&self) -> usize`: Gets the capacity (in bytes) required for the encoded data. This is to avoid double-allocation of memory needed for the encoding. It can be an estimate and does not need to be an exact number. If the size is not known, even no good maximum, then we can skip this function from the trait implementation. This is required to be a cheap operation, so should not involve iterations etc.
- `encode_to<T: Output>(&self, dest: &mut T)`: Encodes the value and appends it to a destination buffer.
- `encode(&self) -> Vec<u8>`: Encodes the type data and returns a slice.
- `using_encoded<R, F: FnOnce(&[u8]) -> R>(&self, f: F) -> R`: Encodes the type data and executes a closure on the encoded value. Returns the result from the executed closure.

**Note:** Implementations should override `using_encoded` for value types and `encode_to` for
allocating types. `size_hint` should be implemented for all types, wherever possible. Wrapper
types should override all methods.

### Decode

The `Decode` trait is used for deserialization/decoding of encoded data into the respective
types.

- `fn decode<I: Input>(value: &mut I) -> Result<Self, Error>`: Tries to decode the value from SCALE format to the type it is called on. Returns an- `Err`if the decoding fails.

### CompactAs

The `CompactAs` trait is used for wrapping custom types/structs as compact types, which makes
them even more space/memory efficient. The compact encoding is described [here](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/scale-codec/#fn-1).

- `encode_as(&self) -> &Self::As`: Encodes the type (self) as a compact type. The type- `As`is defined in the same trait and its implementation should be compact encode-able.
- `decode_from(_: Self::As) -> Result<Self, Error>`: Decodes the type (self) from a compact encode-able type.

### HasCompact

The `HasCompact` trait, if implemented, tells that the corresponding type is a compact
encode-able type.

### EncodeLike

The `EncodeLike` trait needs to be implemented for each type manually. When using derive, it is
done automatically for you. Basically the trait gives you the opportunity to accept multiple
types to a function that all encode to the same representation.

## Usage Examples

Following are some examples to demonstrate usage of the codec.

### Simple types

```
# // Import macros if derive feature is not used.
#
# use ;
use ;
let a = A;
let b = B;
let c = C ;
a.using_encoded;
b.using_encoded;
c.using_encoded;
let mut da: & = b"\x0f";
assert_eq!;
let mut db: & = b"\x01\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0";
assert_eq!;
let mut dc: & = b"\x02\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0";
assert_eq!;
let mut dz: & = &;
assert_eq!;
#
```
### Compact type with HasCompact

```
# // Import macros if derive feature is not used.
#
# use ;
use ;
let test_val:  = ;
let encoded = Test1HasCompact .encode;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
#
```
### Type with CompactAs

```
# // Import macros if derive feature is not used.
#
# use ;
use ;
use ;
;
let a =  ;
let encoded = a.encode;
assert_eq!;
#
```
## Derive attributes

The derive implementation supports the following attributes:

- `codec(dumb_trait_bound)`: This attribute needs to be placed above the type that one of the trait should be implemented for. It will make the algorithm that determines the to-add trait bounds fall back to just use the type parameters of the type. This can be useful for situation where the algorithm includes private types in the public interface. By using this attribute, you should not get this error/warning again.
- `codec(skip)`: Needs to be placed above a field or variant and makes it to be skipped while encoding/decoding.
- `codec(compact)`: Needs to be placed above a field and makes the field use compact encoding. (The type needs to support compact encoding.)
- `codec(encoded_as = "OtherType")`: Needs to be placed above a field and makes the field being encoded by using- `OtherType`.
- `codec(index = 0)`: Needs to be placed above an enum variant to make the variant use the given index when encoded. By default the index is determined by counting from- `0`beginning wth the first variant.
- `codec(encode_bound)`,- `codec(decode_bound)`and- `codec(mel_bound)`: All 3 attributes take in a- `where`clause for the- `Encode`,- `Decode`and- `MaxEncodedLen`trait implementation for the annotated type respectively.
- `codec(encode_bound(skip_type_params))`,- `codec(decode_bound(skip_type_params))`and- `codec(mel_bound(skip_type_params))`: All 3 sub-attributes take in types as arguments to skip trait derivation of the corresponding trait, e.g. T in- `codec(encode_bound(skip_type_params(T)))`will not contain a- `Encode`trait bound while- `Encode`is being derived for the annotated type.

## Known issues

Even though this crate supports deserialization of arbitrarily sized array (e.g. `[T; 1024 * 1024 * 1024]`)
using such types is not recommended and will most likely result in a stack overflow. If you have a big
array inside of your structure which you want to decode you should wrap it in a `Box`, e.g. `Box<[T; 1024 * 1024 * 1024]>`.

# impl-trait-for-tuples 0.2.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/impl-trait-for-tuples/^0.2.2

# impl-trait-for-tuples

Attribute macro to implement a trait for tuples

## Introduction

When wanting to implement a trait for combinations of tuples, Rust requires the trait to be implemented
for each combination manually. With this crate you just need to place `#[impl_for_tuples(5)]` above
your trait declaration (in full-automatic mode) to implement the trait for the tuple combinations
`(), (T0), (T0, T1), (T0, T1, T2), (T0, T1, T2, T3), (T0, T1, T2, T3, T4, T5)`. The number of tuples is the
parameter given to the attribute and can be chosen freely.

This crate provides two modes full-automatic and semi-automatic. The full-automatic mode just requires
the trait definition to implement the trait for the tuple combinations. While being much easier to
use, it also comes with some restrictions like no associated types, no return values or no associated
consts. To support these, the semi-automatic mode is provided. This mode requires a dummy implementation
block of the trait that is expanded to all the tuple combinations implementations. To express the
tuple access in this dummy implementation a special syntax is required `for_tuples!( #( Tuple::function(); )* )`.
This would expand to `Tuple::function();` for each tuple while `Tuple` is chosen by the user and will be
replaced by the corresponding tuple identifier per iteration.

## Syntax

The attribute macro can be called with one `#[impl_for_tuples(5)]` or with two `#[impl_for_tuples(2, 5)]`
parameters. The former instructs the macro to generate up to a tuple of five elements and the later instructs it
to generate from a tuple with two element up to five elements.

### Semi-automatic syntax

```
```
The given example shows all supported combinations of `for_tuples!`. When accessing a method from the
`self` tuple instance, `self.Tuple` is the required syntax and is replaced by `self.0`, `self.1`, etc.
The placeholder tuple identifer is taken from the self type given to the implementation block. So, it
is up to the user to chose any valid identifier.

The separator given to `#( Tuple::something() )SEPARATOR*` can be chosen from `,`, `+`, `-`,
`*`, `/`, `|`, `&` or nothing for no separator.

By adding the `#[tuple_types_no_default_trait_bound]` above the impl block, the macro will not add the
automatic bound to the implemented trait for each tuple type.

The trait bound can be customized using `#[tuple_types_custom_trait_bound(NewBound)]`.
The new bound will be used instead of the impleted trait for each tuple type.

## Limitations

The macro does not supports `for_tuples!` calls in a different macro, so stuff like
`vec![ for_tuples!( bla ) ]` will generate invalid code.

### Full-automatic

```
```
### Semi-automatic

# log 0.4.33 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/log/^0.4.22

# log

A Rust library providing a lightweight logging *facade*.

A logging facade provides a single logging API that abstracts over the actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

## Minimum supported `rustc`

See the `rust-version` field in `Cargo.toml` for the current minimum Rust toolchain version.

This version is explicitly tested in CI and may be bumped in any release as needed. Maintaining compatibility with older compilers is a priority though, so the bar for bumping the minimum supported version is set very high. Any changes to the supported minimum version will be called out in the release notes.

## Usage

### In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided macros to
log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
```
use ;
```
### In executables

In order to produce log output, executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some options:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct [an FFI-safe wrapper over](https://github.com/rust-lang/log/issues/421)to initialize in your libraries.`log`

- You may need to construct
- Utilities:

Executables should choose a logger implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logger implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the logger is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

## Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature, you can associate structured data with your log records:

```
use ;
```

# wasmtime 36.0.12 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasmtime/^36.0.7

A Bytecode Alliance project

## About

This crate is the Rust embedding API for the [Wasmtime](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime) project: a
cross-platform engine for running WebAssembly programs. Notable features of
Wasmtime are:

-
**Fast**. Wasmtime is built on the optimizing[Cranelift](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/blob/main/cranelift/README.md)code generator to quickly generate high-quality machine code either at runtime or ahead-of-time. Wasmtime's runtime is also optimized for cases such as efficient instantiation, low-overhead transitions between the embedder and wasm, and scalability of concurrent instances.
-
[Secure](https://docs.wasmtime.dev/security.html)[Google's OSS Fuzz](https://google.github.io/oss-fuzz/), leveraging Rust's API and runtime safety guarantees, careful design of features and APIs through an[RFC process](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/rfcs), a[security policy](https://bytecodealliance.org/security)in place for when things go wrong, and a[release policy](https://docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-release.html)for patching older versions as well. We follow best practices for defense-in-depth and known protections and mitigations for issues like Spectre. Finally, we're working to push the state-of-the-art by collaborating with academic researchers to formally verify critical parts of Wasmtime and Cranelift.
-
[Configurable](https://docs.rs/wasmtime/latest/wasmtime/struct.Config.html)
-
[WASI](https://docs.rs/wasmtime-wasi/latest/wasmtime_wasi/)[WASI standard](https://wasi.dev).
-
[Standards Compliant](https://docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-wasm-proposals.html)[official WebAssembly test suite](https://github.com/WebAssembly/testsuite), implements the[official C API of wasm](https://github.com/WebAssembly/wasm-c-api), and implements[future proposals to WebAssembly](https://github.com/WebAssembly/proposals)as well. Wasmtime developers are intimately engaged with the WebAssembly standards process all along the way too.

## Example

An example of using the Wasmtime embedding API for running a small WebAssembly module might look like:

```
use Result;
use *;
```
More examples and information can be found in the `wasmtime` crate's [online
documentation](https://docs.rs/wasmtime) as well.

## Documentation

The [wasmtime guide](https://bytecodealliance.github.io/wasmtime) is the best starting point to learn about what
Wasmtime can do for you or help answer your questions about Wasmtime. If you're
curious in contributing to Wasmtime, [it can also help you do
that](https://bytecodealliance.github.io/wasmtime/contributing.html)!

For information on supported versions of Wasmtime see [the corresponding online book
documentation](https://docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-release.html#current-versions).

# anyhow 1.0.103 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/anyhow/1.0.103

# Anyhow ¯\_(°ペ)_/¯

This library provides [ anyhow::Error](https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0/anyhow/struct.Error.html), a trait object based error type
for easy idiomatic error handling in Rust applications.

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Details

-
Use `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`, or equivalently`anyhow::Result<T>`, as the return type of any fallible function.Within the function, use `?`to easily propagate any error that implements the`std::error::Error``use Result;`
-
Attach context to help the person troubleshooting the error understand where things went wrong. A low-level error like "No such file or directory" can be annoying to debug without more context about what higher level step the application was in the middle of. `use ;``Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
-
Downcasting is supported and can be by value, by shared reference, or by mutable reference as needed. `// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a // tombstone instead of the content. match root_cause.`
-
If using Rust ≥ 1.65, a backtrace is captured and printed with the error if the underlying error type does not already provide its own. In order to see backtraces, they must be enabled through the environment variables described in `std::backtrace`- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only errors to have backtraces, set `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only panics to have backtraces, set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`and`RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`.

- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
-
Anyhow works with any error type that has an impl of `std::error::Error`, including ones defined in your crate. We do not bundle a`derive(Error)`macro but you can write the impls yourself or use a standalone macro like[thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror).`use Error;`
-
One-off error messages can be constructed using the `anyhow!`macro, which supports string interpolation and produces an`anyhow::Error`.`return Err;`A `bail!`macro is provided as a shorthand for the same early return.`bail!;`

## No-std support

In no_std mode, almost all of the same API is available and works the same way. To depend on Anyhow in no_std mode, disable our default enabled "std" feature in Cargo.toml. A global allocator is required.

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0",  = false }
```
With versions of Rust older than 1.81, no_std mode may require an additional
`.map_err(Error::msg)` when working with a non-Anyhow error type inside a
function that returns Anyhow's error type, as the trait that `?`-based error
conversions are defined by is only available in std in those old versions.

## Comparison to failure

The `anyhow::Error` type works something like `failure::Error`, but unlike
failure ours is built around the standard library's `std::error::Error` trait
rather than a separate trait `failure::Fail`. The standard library has adopted
the necessary improvements for this to be possible as part of [RFC 2504](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/2504-fix-error.md).

## Comparison to thiserror

Use Anyhow if you don't care what error type your functions return, you just
want it to be easy. This is common in application code. Use [thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror) if you
are a library that wants to design your own dedicated error type(s) so that on
failures the caller gets exactly the information that you choose.

---

# futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3/

## Expand description

Abstractions for asynchronous programming.

This crate provides a number of core abstractions for writing asynchronous code:

- [Futures](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)are single eventual values produced by asynchronous computations. Some programming languages (e.g. JavaScript) call this concept “promise”.
- [Streams](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)represent a series of values produced asynchronously.
- [Sinks](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html)provide support for asynchronous writing of data.
- [Executors](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)are responsible for running asynchronous tasks.

The crate also contains abstractions for [asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) and
[cross-task communication](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html).

Underlying all of this is the *task system*, which is a form of lightweight
threading. Large asynchronous computations are built up using futures,
streams and sinks, and then spawned as independent tasks that are run to
completion, but *do not block* the thread running them.

The following example describes how the task system context is built and used within macros and keywords such as async and await!.

```
fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new().expect("Failed to build pool");
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::unbounded::<i32>();
    // Create a future by an async block, where async is responsible for an
    // implementation of Future. At this point no executor has been provided
    // to this future, so it will not be running.
    let fut_values = async {
        // Create another async block, again where the Future implementation
        // is generated by async. Since this is inside of a parent async block,
        // it will be provided with the executor of the parent block when the parent
        // block is executed.
        //
        // This executor chaining is done by Future::poll whose second argument
        // is a std::task::Context. This represents our executor, and the Future
        // implemented by this async block can be polled using the parent async
        // block's executor.
        let fut_tx_result = async move {
            (0..100).for_each(|v| {
                tx.unbounded_send(v).expect("Failed to send");
            })
        };
        // Use the provided thread pool to spawn the generated future
        // responsible for transmission
        pool.spawn_ok(fut_tx_result);
        let fut_values = rx
            .map(|v| v * 2)
            .collect();
        // Use the executor provided to this async block to wait for the
        // future to complete.
        fut_values.await
    };
    // Actually execute the above future, which will invoke Future::poll and
    // subsequently chain appropriate Future::poll and methods needing executors
    // to drive all futures. Eventually fut_values will be driven to completion.
    let values: Vec<i32> = executor::block_on(fut_values);
    println!("Values={:?}", values);
}
```
The majority of examples and code snippets in this crate assume that they are inside an async block as written above.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, returning a tuple of all results once complete.
- [pending](https://docs.rs/macro.pending.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which yields to the event loop once.
- [pin_mut](https://docs.rs/macro.pin_mut.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/macro.poll.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which returns the result of polling a future once within the
current `async`context.
- [ready](https://docs.rs/macro.ready.html)
- Extracts the successful type of `Poll<T>`.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `async-await`and- `std`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. If multiple futures are ready,
one will be pseudo-randomly selected at runtime. Futures directly
passed to `select!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/macro.select_biased.html)- biased - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. Unlike `select!``select_biased!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/macro.stream_select.html)- select - `async-await`and- `std`
- Combines several streams, all producing the same `Item`type, into one stream. This is similar to`select_all`but does not require the streams to all be the same type. It also keeps the streams inline, and does not require`Box<dyn Stream>`s to be allocated. Streams passed to this macro must be`Unpin`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, resolving to a `Result`

# rustversion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustversion/^1.0.6/

## Expand description

This crate provides macros for conditional compilation according to rustc
compiler version, analogous to [ #[cfg(...)]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg-attribute) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg_attr-attribute)

`#[cfg_attr(...)]`[§](https://docs.rs#selectors)Selectors

- `#[rustversion::stable]`
 True on any stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::stable(1.34)]`
 True on exactly the specified stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::beta]`
 True on any beta compiler.
- `#[rustversion::nightly]`
 True on any nightly compiler or dev build.
- `#[rustversion::nightly(2025-01-01)]`
 True on exactly one nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(1.34)]`
 True on that stable release and any later compiler, including beta and nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(2025-01-01)]`
 True on that nightly and all newer ones.
- `#[rustversion::before(`- *version or date*- `)]`
 Negative of- *#[rustversion::since(...)]*.
- `#[rustversion::not(`- *selector*- `)]`
 Negative of any selector; for example- *#[rustversion::not(nightly)]*.
- `#[rustversion::any(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if any of the comma-separated selectors is true; for example- *#[rustversion::any(stable, beta)]*.
- `#[rustversion::all(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if all of the comma-separated selectors are true; for example- *#[rustversion::all(since(1.31), before(1.34))]*.
- `#[rustversion::attr(`- *selector*- `,`- *attribute*- `)]`
 For conditional inclusion of attributes; analogous to- `cfg_attr`.
- `rustversion::cfg!(`- *selector*- `)`
 An expression form of any of the above attributes; for example- *if rustversion::cfg!(any(stable, beta)) { ... }*.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-cases)Use cases

Providing additional trait impls as types are stabilized in the standard library
without breaking compatibility with older compilers; in this case Pin<P>
stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2019/02/28/Rust-1.33.0.html#pinning):

```
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
use std::pin::Pin;
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
impl<P: MyTrait> MyTrait for Pin<P> {
    /* ... */
}
```
Similar but for language features; the ability to control alignment greater than
1 of packed structs was stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/RELEASES.md#version-1330-2019-02-28).

```
#[rustversion::attr(before(1.33), repr(packed))]
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.33), repr(packed(2)))]
struct Six(i16, i32);
fn main() {
    println!("{}", std::mem::align_of::<Six>());
}
```
Augmenting code with `const` as const impls are stabilized in the standard
library. This use of `const` as an attribute is recognized as a special case
by the rustversion::attr macro.

```
use std::time::Duration;
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.32), const)]
fn duration_as_days(dur: Duration) -> u64 {
    dur.as_secs() / 60 / 60 / 24
}
```
Emitting Cargo cfg directives from a build script. Note that this requires
listing `rustversion` under `[build-dependencies]` in Cargo.toml, not
`[dependencies]`.

```
// build.rs
fn main() {
    if rustversion::cfg!(since(1.36)) {
        println!("cargo:rustc-cfg=no_std");
    }
}
```
```
// src/lib.rs
#![cfg_attr(no_std, no_std)]
#[cfg(no_std)]
extern crate alloc;
```

---

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2.0/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Abi](https://docs.rs/struct.Abi.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The binary interface of a function: `extern "C"`.
- [Angle](https://docs.rs/struct.AngleBracketedGenericArguments.html)- Bracketed - Generic - Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed arguments of a path segment: the `<K, V>`in`HashMap<K, V>`.
- [Arm](https://docs.rs/struct.Arm.html)- `full`
- One arm of a `match`expression:`0..=10 => { return true; }`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocConst.html)- Const - `derive`or- `full`
- An equality constraint on an associated constant: the `PANIC = false`in`Trait<PANIC = false>`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- A binding (equality constraint) on an associated type: the `Item = u8`in`Iterator<Item = u8>`.
- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/struct.Attribute.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An attribute, like `#[repr(transparent)]`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareFnArg.html)- FnArg - `derive`or- `full`
- An argument in a function type: the `usize`in`fn(usize) -> bool`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareVariadic.html)- Variadic - `derive`or- `full`
- The variadic argument of a function pointer like `fn(usize, ...)`.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.Block.html)- `full`
- A braced block containing Rust statements.
- [Bound](https://docs.rs/struct.BoundLifetimes.html)- Lifetimes - `derive`or- `full`
- A set of bound lifetimes: `for<'a, 'b, 'c>`.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A const generic parameter: `const LENGTH: usize`.
- [Constraint](https://docs.rs/struct.Constraint.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An associated type bound: `Iterator<Item: Display>`.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataEnum.html)- Enum - `derive`
- An enum input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataStruct.html)- Struct - `derive`
- A struct input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataUnion.html)- Union - `derive`
- An untagged union input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Derive](https://docs.rs/struct.DeriveInput.html)- Input - `derive`
- Data structure sent to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error returned when a Syn parser cannot parse the input tokens.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprArray.html)- Array - `full`
- A slice literal expression: `[a, b, c, d]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAssign.html)- Assign - `full`
- An assignment expression: `a = compute()`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAsync.html)- Async - `full`
- An async block: `async { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAwait.html)- Await - `full`
- An await expression: `fut.await`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBinary.html)- Binary - `derive`or- `full`
- A binary operation: `a + b`,`a += b`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBlock.html)- Block - `full`
- A blocked scope: `{ ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBreak.html)- Break - `full`
- A `break`, with an optional label to break and an optional expression.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCall.html)- Call - `derive`or- `full`
- A function call expression: `invoke(a, b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCast.html)- Cast - `derive`or- `full`
- A cast expression: `foo as f64`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprClosure.html)- Closure - `full`
- A closure expression: `|a, b| a + b`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprConst.html)- Const - `full`
- A const block: `const { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprContinue.html)- Continue - `full`
- A `continue`, with an optional label.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprField.html)- Field - `derive`or- `full`
- Access of a named struct field (`obj.k`) or unnamed tuple struct field (`obj.0`).
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprForLoop.html)- ForLoop - `full`
- A for loop: `for pat in expr { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprGroup.html)- Group - `full`
- An expression contained within invisible delimiters.
- [ExprIf](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprIf.html)- `full`
- An `if`expression with an optional`else`block:`if expr { ... } else { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprIndex.html)- Index - `derive`or- `full`
- A square bracketed indexing expression: `vector[2]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprInfer.html)- Infer - `full`
- The inferred value of a const generic argument, denoted `_`.
- [ExprLet](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLet.html)- `full`
- A `let`guard:`let Some(x) = opt`.
- [ExprLit](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLit.html)- `derive`or- `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLoop.html)- Loop - `full`
- Conditionless loop: `loop { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMacro.html)- Macro - `derive`or- `full`
- A macro invocation expression: `format!("{}", q)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMatch.html)- Match - `full`
- A `match`expression:`match n { Some(n) => {}, None => {} }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMethodCall.html)- Method - Call - `derive`or- `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprParen.html)- Paren - `derive`or- `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprPath.html)- Path - `derive`or- `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRange.html)- Range - `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRepeat.html)- Repeat - `full`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Attr](https://docs.rs/enum.AttrStyle.html)- Style - `derive`or- `full`
- Distinguishes between attributes that decorate an item and attributes that are contained within an item.
- [BinOp](https://docs.rs/enum.BinOp.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A binary operator: `+`,`+=`,`&`.
- [Captured](https://docs.rs/enum.CapturedParam.html)- Param - `full`
- Single parameter in a precise capturing bound.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/enum.Data.html)- `derive`
- The storage of a struct, enum or union data structure.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A Rust expression.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/enum.FieldMutability.html)- Mutability - `derive`or- `full`
- Unused, but reserved for RFC 3323 restrictions.
- [Fields](https://docs.rs/enum.Fields.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Data stored within an enum variant or struct.
- [FnArg](https://docs.rs/enum.FnArg.html)- `full`
- An argument in a function signature: the `n: usize`in`fn f(n: usize)`.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/enum.ForeignItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item within an `extern`block.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/enum.GenericArgument.html)- Argument - `derive`or- `full`
- An individual generic argument, like `'a`,`T`, or`Item = T`.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/enum.GenericParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A generic type parameter, lifetime, or const generic: `T: Into<String>`,`'a: 'b`,`const LEN: usize`.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/enum.ImplItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item within an impl block.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/enum.ImplRestriction.html)- Restriction - `full`
- Unused, but reserved for RFC 3323 restrictions.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/enum.Item.html)- `full`
- Things that can appear directly inside of a module or scope.
- [Lit](https://docs.rs/enum.Lit.html)
- A Rust literal such as a string or integer or boolean.
- [Macro](https://docs.rs/enum.MacroDelimiter.html)- Delimiter - `derive`or- `full`
- A grouping token that surrounds a macro body: `m!(...)`or`m!{...}`or`m![...]`.
- [Member](https://docs.rs/enum.Member.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A struct or tuple struct field accessed in a struct literal or field expression.
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/enum.Meta.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Content of a compile-time structured attribute.
- [Pat](https://docs.rs/enum.Pat.html)- `full`
- A pattern in a local binding, function signature, match expression, or various other places.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/enum.PathArguments.html)- Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed or parenthesized arguments of a path segment.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/enum.PointerMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- Mutability of a raw pointer (`*const T`,`*mut T`), in which non-mutable isn’t the implicit default.
- [Range](https://docs.rs/enum.RangeLimits.html)- Limits - `full`
- Limit types of a range, inclusive or exclusive.
- [Return](https://docs.rs/enum.ReturnType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- Return type of a function signature.
- [Static](https://docs.rs/enum.StaticMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- The mutability of an `Item::Static`or`ForeignItem::Static`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/enum.Stmt.html)- `full`
- A statement, usually ending in a semicolon.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitBoundModifier.html)- Bound - Modifier - `derive`or- `full`
- A modifier on a trait bound, currently only used for the `?`in`?Sized`.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item declaration within the definition of a trait.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.Type.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The possible types that a Rust value could have.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeParamBound.html)- Param - Bound - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait or lifetime used as a bound on a type parameter.
- [UnOp](https://docs.rs/enum.UnOp.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A unary operator: `*`,`!`,`-`.
- [UseTree](https://docs.rs/enum.UseTree.html)- `full`
- A suffix of an import tree in a `use`item:`Type as Renamed`or`*`.
- [Visibility](https://docs.rs/enum.Visibility.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The visibility level of an item: inherited or `pub`or`pub(restricted)`.
- [Where](https://docs.rs/enum.WherePredicate.html)- Predicate - `derive`or- `full`
- A single predicate in a `where`clause:`T: Deserialize<'de>`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)- `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse tokens of source code into the chosen syntax tree node.
- [parse2](https://docs.rs/fn.parse2.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a proc-macro2 token stream into the chosen syntax tree node.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_file.html)- file - `full`and- `parsing`
- Parse the content of a file of Rust code.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_str.html)- str - `parsing`
- Parse a string of Rust code into the chosen syntax tree node.

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- The result of a Syn parser.
